title: Adiabatic Process in Thermodynamics
short_intro: An adiabatic process is a thermodynamic process in which no heat is exchanged between a system and its surroundings (dQ = 0). During this process, changes in internal energy result entirely from work done by or on the system.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of adiabatic process, first law of thermodynamics applied to dQ = 0, Poisson's relations between P, V, and T, work done during adiabatic expansion and compression, and comparison of adiabatic and isothermal slopes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Microscopic derivation of Poisson's law using the equipartition of energy and degrees of freedom, adiabatic elasticity of gases, free expansion of ideal and real gases (Joule-Thomson effect), and velocity of sound in air (Newton-Laplace formula).

prerequisites: Concept of Temperature and First Law of Thermodynamics
Degrees of Freedom and Law of Equipartition of Energy
Equation of State for Ideal Gases (PV = nRT)

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Definition and First Law Form
bullets: By definition, an adiabatic process satisfies the condition dQ = 0 (no heat enters or leaves the system).
Applying the First Law of Thermodynamics (dU = dQ - dW), for an adiabatic process, dU = -dW.
If a gas expands adiabatically (dW > 0), its internal energy decreases (dU < 0), causing a drop in temperature.

concept_notes.heading: Poisson's Relations for Ideal Gases
bullets: For an ideal gas undergoing a reversible adiabatic process, the variables are related by PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant, where γ = C<sub>p</sub> / C<sub>v</sub> is the adiabatic index.
Alternative forms include TV<sup>γ-1</sup> = constant and P<sup>1-γ</sup>T<sup>γ</sup> = constant.
The value of γ depends strictly on the atomicity (degrees of freedom) of the gas: γ = 1.67 for monatomic, γ = 1.40 for diatomic, and γ = 1.33 for polyatomic gases.

concept_notes.heading: Comparison with Isothermal Processes
bullets: In an isothermal process, temperature remains constant (dT = 0), and PV = constant.
In an adiabatic process, pressure changes more rapidly with volume because the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve by a factor of γ.
The slope of the adiabatic curve on a P-V diagram is given by (dP/dV)<sub>ad</sub> = -γ (P/V), whereas the isothermal slope is (dP/dV)<sub>iso</sub> = -(P/V).

concept_notes.heading: Adiabatic Elasticity of Gases
bullets: The bulk modulus of elasticity for a gas undergoing an isothermal process is equal to its pressure P.
For an adiabatic process, differentiating PV<sup>γ</sup> = constant yields the adiabatic elasticity E<sub>ad</sub> = γP.
This higher rigidity modulus is directly utilized in Laplace's correction for the velocity of sound in gases.

derivations.title: Derivation of Poisson's Law (PV^gamma = constant)
derivations.conditions: Reversible adiabatic process for an ideal gas
steps: Start with the First Law of Thermodynamics: dQ = dU + dW. For an adiabatic process, dQ = 0, so dU + dW = 0.
Substitute dU = n C_v dT and dW = P dV into the equation: n C_v dT + P dV = 0.
Use the ideal gas equation, PV = nRT, and differentiate it: P dV + V dP = n R dT, which gives dT = (P dV + V dP) / (nR).
Substitute dT into the energy equation: n C_v [(P dV + V dP) / (nR)] + P dV = 0. Since R = C_p - C_v, let C_p / C_v = gamma.
Divide by C_v and simplify to obtain (P dV + V dP) / (gamma - 1) + P dV = 0, which reduces to V dP + gamma P dV = 0.
Divide the entire equation by PV to get (dP / P) + gamma (dV / V) = 0.
Integrating both sides yields ln P + gamma ln V = constant, leading directly to PV^gamma = constant.

derivations.title: Work Done in an Adiabatic Process
derivations.conditions: Quasistatic adiabatic expansion or compression of an ideal gas from (P_1, V_1, T_1) to (P_2, V_2, T_2)
steps: The work done in any thermodynamic process is given by W = int_{V_1}^{V_2} P dV.
For an adiabatic process, PV^gamma = K (constant), so P = K / V^gamma.
Substitute P into the integral: W = int_{V_1}^{V_2} (K / V^gamma) dV = K int_{V_1}^{V_2} V^{-gamma} dV.
Evaluate the integral: W = K [ (V_2^{1-gamma} - V_1^{1-gamma}) / (1 - gamma) ].
Since K = P_1 V_1^gamma = P_2 V_2^gamma, substitute K at the respective limits: W = [ (P_2 V_2^gamma V_2^{1-gamma} - P_1 V_1^gamma V_1^{1-gamma}) / (1 - gamma) ].
Simplify the expression to obtain W = (P_1 V_1 - P_2 V_2) / (gamma - 1).

graphs_and_experiments.title: P-V Diagram Comparing Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A set of curves on a P-V plane starting from the same initial state (P_1, V_1). The adiabatic curve drops faster and lies below the isothermal curve during expansion.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The adiabatic curve has a slope γ times steeper than the isothermal curve because heat cannot enter to sustain the temperature during expansion.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in multiple-choice questions regarding work done, final temperatures, and curve steepness.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Clement and Desormes' Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of a large glass flask connected to a manometer and a pump, demonstrating adiabatic expansion of air.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Used to determine the ratio of specific heats (γ) of a gas by noting pressure changes during sudden opening and closing of a stopcock.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Core experimental setup for PGT physics practical theory questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Adiabatic Free Expansion (Joule Effect)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Two insulated bulbs connected by a valve; one contains gas at pressure P, the other is evacuated.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: When the valve opens, the gas expands into vacuum without doing external work (W = 0) and without heat exchange (Q = 0), resulting in dU = 0.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used to test conceptual understanding of internal energy dependence on temperature for ideal versus real gases.

solved_numericals.question: A certain mass of an ideal gas (? = 1.4) is compressed adiabatically from an initial volume of 8 liters to 1 liter. If the initial pressure is 1 atm, find the final pressure.
solution_steps: Identify given data: V_1 = 8 L, V_2 = 1 L, P_1 = 1 atm, gamma = 1.4.
Apply Poisson's law for pressure and volume: P_1 V_1^gamma = P_2 V_2^gamma.

solved_numericals.question: Two moles of an ideal monatomic gas (? = 5/3) at 300 K are compressed adiabatically and reversibly to half of their initial volume. Calculate the final temperature and the work done on the gas.
solution_steps: Identify given data: n = 2, T_1 = 300 K, V_2 / V_1 = 1/2, gamma = 5/3.
Use the temperature-volume relation: T_1 V_1^{gamma-1} = T_2 V_2^{gamma-1}.
Using R = 8.314 J/mol·K, W = -3 * 8.314 * 176.1 approx -4393 J. Work done on the gas is +4393 J.
solved_numericals.answer: Final Temperature = 476.1 K, Work done on the gas = 4393 J

solved_numericals.question: Find the adiabatic elasticity of a diatomic gas (? = 1.4) kept at a normal atmospheric pressure of 1.013 × 10^5 N/m^2.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for adiabatic elasticity: E_{ad} = gamma P.
Substitute the given values: gamma = 1.4 and P = 1.013 × 10^5 N/m^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: The process must be perfectly insulated (dQ = 0), which is practically difficult to achieve as complete thermal isolation does not exist.
For the relations PV^gamma = constant to hold, the process must be quasistatic (infinitely slow) so that the system remains in internal thermal and mechanical equilibrium at all intermediate stages.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An adiabatic process must always be sudden.
common_misconceptions.correct: An adiabatic process can be carried out either rapidly or slowly, provided the system is thermally insulated from its surroundings.
common_misconceptions.why: Rapidity ensures no heat exchange due to time constraints, but even a slow process is adiabatic if the boundaries are perfectly lagging (insulated).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Temperature remains constant during an adiabatic expansion because no heat is added.
common_misconceptions.why: Since dQ = 0 and the gas does positive work (dW > 0), the internal energy must decrease (dU < 0), directly leading to a drop in temperature.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The adiabatic exponent gamma is a universal constant for all gases.
common_misconceptions.correct: The value of gamma depends entirely on the atomicity and degrees of freedom of the specific gas.
common_misconceptions.why: gamma = 1 + (2/f) where f is the degrees of freedom, which varies between monatomic, diatomic, and polyatomic molecules.

quick_revision: Adiabatic curves are steeper than isothermal curves by a factor of gamma.
Work done in adiabatic expansion: W = (P_1V_1 - P_2V_2) / (gamma - 1).
Laplace's correction uses adiabatic bulk modulus E_{ad} = gamma P for sound velocity in gases.
